title: Why science belongs here
hookLine: science can't tell you what's sacred, but it can tell you what tends to help

lines: TEN MINUTES AND ANXIETY IS GONE.
cards: Scroll any feed for a minute and someone will promise you something. Ten minutes of this breathing and your anxiety is gone. This ancient ritual rewires your brain.
Monks have known this for centuries, and now science agrees. Some of those claims are true, some are half true, and some are made up to sell a course.
On a path that borrows from Stoics and Sufis and Zen teachers, it's fair to ask: how would anyone know which practices help? This week, the science of practice.

teach.b: Start with what science can't do.
It can't tell you what's sacred, whether God exists, what a life is for, or whom you should love. Those are questions for traditions, philosophy and your own conscience.

The biologist Stephen Jay Gould argued that science and religion answer different kinds of questions; not everyone agrees with how he drew the line, but the basic point holds. A lab can't weigh meaning.
Now what science can do. It can test whether a practice tends to help with something measurable: sleep, stress, attention, mood, pain.

It can compare people who practice with people who don't, and see if the difference is real or just chance. That's worth knowing, because practices cost time, some cost money, and some claims are simply wrong.
This isn't new on this path.

Back in 1890, the American psychologist William James opened his huge book on the mind with a plain definition: "Psychology is the Science of Mental Life, both of its phenomena and of their conditions."
Twelve years later, in 1902, he turned the same curious, careful eye on religious experience itself, respectfully, without trying to explain it away. So here are my rules for this week.

teach.h: NAME IT, SIZE IT, COMPARE IT.
teach.b: I'll name every study, say how big it was, and say what it compared. I'll say plainly when results are modest, mixed or unknown. And I'll never claim a lab has settled your faith, for or against.
What it can offer is humbler, and useful: some honest evidence about what tends to help.

how: Researchers in psychology and medicine study contemplative practices with trials and surveys, and many practitioners use the findings to choose what to keep without treating them as a verdict on faith.

practice: Think back over the practices on this path: watching the breath, the evening review, gratitude, walking, the digital sabbath.
Which one have you actually kept, even a little, and which one have you wondered about: does this really do anything? Hold one of them in mind like a question you'll carry into this week.

wordCard.voice: Scientia, the Latin root of science: it can't say what's sacred, but it can test what tends to help, and keeps us honest.
